title: [client-go] add a pod-logs example
body:
**What would you like to be added?** I'd like to add a new pod-logs example to [INLINE_CODE]. It's a simple script that lists pods across namespaces and streams the last few lines of their container logs to the terminal.

**Why is this needed?** I noticed we don't actually have a basic "how to get pod logs" example. It's such a common thing for people to do, but there isn't a dedicated example yet!

Proposal: Make pod log endpoint more useful. the pod log endpoint on the apiserver and kubelet was implemented as a simple wrapper around docker logs. it's intended to provide easy access for users and administrators to the logs of the currently running execution of a container in a pod. if there is no running execution, it will show the last execution. there are two flags supported : - [ inline _ code ] instructs docker to leave the connection open and stream new changes until the container exits or the log connection is closed by the consumer - [ inline _ code ] uses the previous execution of the container to display logs when not following logs, the default docker behavior of returning the entire log file is preserved ( docker [ inline _ code ] ). we currently suppress the timestamp shown by docker ( because the logs may already contain timestamps ). # # problems today : - a container may generate many megabytes of logs which must be transferred to the client every time the user runs'logs'- a container running for several days may generate periodic logs, but a user is only interested in the last few hours - a user may wish to see when a log statement was generated, but not have added timestamps to their logs themselves types of containers and typical uses : 1. run - once containers are typically used to run jobs - for most users, seeing the entire log of a completed job is useful, or watching the logs until their fail 2. run - forever containers are usually used to run services - users typically : 1. want to debug something that has happened recently, or watch for something that has already happened 2. want to analyze their logs across a larger band of time by searching / scanning for particular behaviors finally, for existing systems there may be log aggregators that provide access to historical logs for a pod / container across multiple attempts or deep history. it would be desirable in the future to be able to abstract access to deep logging in a way that clients can remain oblivious. # # consuming use cases - openshift is looking to expose log retrieval / scanning via its web console - openshift is looking to integrate elasticsearch so that it can be used for multi - tenant historical log retrieval, with a simple integration ( via the existing log apis ) and then for all other queries via a secured proxy that imposes query restrictions to the elastic search api. # # suggested changes to better support clients that want to handle limiting the amount

title: Graduate old Alpha metrics to Beta
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Before introduction of Beta metric stability, we had many important metrics that were stuck in Alpha state.

Would like to propose a list of metric candidates that should be reviewed for graduation to Beta.

We would still review each metric individually for any antipattern, but fact they are in use for so long should be good enough reason for graduation. 

Graduation criteria are at https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/9de615daee15bdee370a825dc0ef150eac189700/contributors/devel/sig-instrumentation/metric-instrumentation.md#graduating-to-beta

Subtasks:
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136304
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136305
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136306
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136307
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136308
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136310
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136311
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136312
* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136313

### Why is this needed?

Those metrics have been already present in K8s for long time and are at use by GKE. 

While we won't necessarily want to graduate them GA, marking them as Beta would indicate their importance and allow community to pay more attention to them over other Alpha metrics.

/cc @richabanker @dgrisonnet

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Readiness Observations & Recommendations (Research)
body:
### What would you like to be added?

This issue shares research-based observations on post-quantum cryptography (PQC) readiness
in Kubernetes, based solely on publicly available code and documentation.

This is NOT a vulnerability report and does not include exploitation, attack paths, or
sensitive configuration details. The intent is awareness, future-readiness, and community
discussion aligned with NIST PQC transition guidance.

Observations:
• Cryptographic usage is distributed across multiple layers
• There is no centralized crypto inventory or ownership map
• No defined crypto agility or PQC migration framework
• No governance-level visibility into algorithm lifecycle

Recommendations:
• Consider adding a crypto inventory layer
• Define crypto ownership and lifecycle policy
• Track NIST PQC migration readiness
• Introduce crypto agility abstractions
• Document PQC roadmap for operators

Why this matters:
Quantum-safe transitions are multi-year efforts. Early visibility reduces long-term risk.

Happy to refine or contribute to documentation if helpful.

### Why is this needed?

Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) transitions are multi-year efforts that require early visibility and planning. 
Today, Kubernetes uses strong cryptography, but cryptographic usage is distributed across many layers 
(control plane, components, SDKs, dependencies), making long-term migration and governance difficult to track.

This enhancement is needed to:
- Improve visibility into cryptographic usage and ownership
- Enable crypto agility and algorithm lifecycle management
- Align Kubernetes with NIST post-quantum transition guidance
- Reduce future migration risk by identifying readiness gaps early
- Support operators and maintainers with clear, documented PQC readiness signals

This is not related to an exploitable vulnerability. 
It is a forward-looking readiness and governance improvement to help Kubernetes remain secure over the next decade.

Consider a kind of Service that ignores readiness. this is mostly motivated by petset. currently we create a governing service that is responsible for the network identity of each pet. the requirements of this governing service differ from a normal service in the following ways : 1. pets have internal protocols to notice peer health, and a list of different checks ( eg : http : / / www. cloudera. com / documentation / enterprise / 5 - 4 - x / topics / cm _ ht _ zookeeper _ server. html ). in kube, peers use dns to communicate. so we don't want a readiness check failure to remove the pet from dns and abruptly cut it off from the set. 2. the " governing service " is headless so kube - proxy doesn't need to nat the service ip. 3. clients will not be using this service, so it doesn't matter that unready pets show up in dns under the svcname sub domain. in addition to these, there's one important reason some pets need to have dns before readiness. to provide the guarantees required to safely bootstrap a pet, we need : 1. pet0 starts before pet1.. 2. don't start pet1 till pet0 is running / ready 3. when pet1 starts, it sees pet0 in dns the easiest way to guarantee 3 today is to do one of : - poll in the entrypoint of pet0, till it sees itself - poll in the init container of pet0, till it sees itself - poll in the init containers of pet { 1.. n - 1 } till it sees all previous pets third option is not a great idea because we don't know who else is supposed to exist, and for the first 2 to work with a readiness probe, we need a dns record before the service is ready.

title: Metrics monitors getter set by DefaultStorageFactory is being overwritten by SimpleStorageFactory
body:
### What happened?

I investigated an issue with etcd storage metrics collection where etcd overrides weren't appearing correctly in the metrics.

Expected behavior: According to the ([implementation](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/metrics/metrics.go#L331)) and ([original intention](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/118812#discussion_r1252695238)), etcd overrides should be configured separately and displayed as etcd-1, etcd-2, etc.

Actual behavior: Only etcd-0 (the base etcd server) appeared in metrics, even when overrides were configured.

Likely Root cause: The monitor getter (which retrieves etcd configs) is set twice:

First by DefaultStorageFactory (includes overrides map)

Then by SimpleStorageFactory (excludes overrides map)

title: Unblock enablement of the ConcurrentWatchObjectDecode by default (to fix scale issues for CRDs)
body:
### What would you like to be added?

[ConcurrentWatchObjectDecode](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/features/kube_features.go#L1955C18-L1957) is currently Beta, but disabled by default.

**I would like to identify or understand the blockers for graduation (if any) so that this can be moved forward.**

This feature gate looks very promising for handling CRD objects with high cardinality, like Workload objects in [Kueue](https://kueue.sigs.k8s.io/). Without this feature gate migration between versions like [INLINE_CODE] to [INLINE_CODE] is risky at scale.

We would love to have this improved before migrating Kueue v1beta2 -> v1.

### Why is this needed?

In Kueue 0.15 we introduced v1beta2 for serving, while keeping v1beta1 for storage. Which was dictated by the needs of downgrading to 0.14 in case something "goes wrong".

However, this caused issues on high scale clusters (small clusters <10k work fine).

My understanding of the problem:
1. when Kueue is starting up then controller-runtime tries to establish the WATCH on the Workload object in v1beta2
2. If the API server does not have a "warm" cache for the Workloads, then it requests ETCD for the list of Workloads in v1beta1
3. API server receives the workloads list, but before returning to Kueue it tries to convert them sequentially to v1beta2. 

**Issue**: for some larger clusters it was estimated to take around 8min, but this exceeds some timeouts in ETCD to serve the request, and the API server fails with 500 in the meanwhile.

There is a good chance that enabling parallel requests would save the request.

**Mitigation**: we recommend users to move from Kueue 0.15 to 0.16 (which is using v1beta2 for storage and serving) which mitigates the problem, but the situation is not ideal, because 0.15 remains affected.

Related issues in Kueue:
- https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/9094
- https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/9145
- https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/9090

title: Investigate capslock for dependency update analysis
body:
https://github.com/google/capslock -- Something GKE Security folks have mentioned.

> Capslock is a capability analysis CLI for Go packages that informs users of which privileged operations a given package can access. This works by classifying the capabilities of Go packages by following transitive calls to privileged standard library operations.

> The recent increase in supply chain attacks targeting open source software has highlighted that third party dependencies should not be inherently trusted. Capabilities indicate what permissions a package has access to, and can be used in conjunction with other security signals to indicate which code requires additional scrutiny before it can be considered trusted.

NOTE: https://github.com/google/capslock/blob/main/docs/caveats.md (particularly the build tags constraint, which generally applies to our Go static analysis tools)

title: etcd watcher scalability or improve decode efficiency
body:
### What would you like to be added?

**Context**
We are developing a Custom Resource Definition (CRD) controller that utilizes the standard list-watch (informer) mechanism. Under high workload conditions, we are observing significant latency in the initial notification trigger for reconciliation loops.

**Observations**
Upon inspecting the Kubernetes API server logs, we identified a high volume of the following warning messages:

`"Fast watcher, slow processing. Probably caused by slow decoding, user not receiving fast, or other processing logic"
`

This suggests a bottleneck where the API server is generating events faster than they can be decoded or consumed. While the log message mentions "slow decoding," our monitoring indicates that the controller itself is not CPU-bound or busy; rather, it appears starved of events because the API server cannot push them efficiently.

**Current Investigation**
We noticed that starting in Kubernetes v1.31, the feature gate ConcurrentWatchObjectDecode was introduced to address decoding bottlenecks by parallelizing the decoding of watch events. However, the current implementation hardcodes the concurrency limit to 10 workers. And the incoming/outgoing bufSize are also hardcoded to 100.

We are seeking the guidance if we could increase the hardcoded settings to improve the watcher efficiency, and whether k8s could provide a feature or guidance how to tune this case, e.g. improve the decoding efficiency.

### Why is this needed?

The controller is being starved of timely updates because the API server cannot produce events efficiently.

similar_issues.text: Create a cache in apiserver to improve its performance. # # background while running kubernetes on 100 - node cluster, the main bottleneck is the apiserver. for example, starting a replication controller with 3000 pods ( 100 nodes, 30 pods per node ) on the empty cluster lasts almost 20 minutes, and the cpu of 4 - core master is 100 % saturated for all that time. looking at the profiles, more than 50 % of cpu is spent on decoding objects coming from etcd ( i. e. decoding jsons ). i don't think we can do much with decoding itself, but what we can do is to limit the number of decodings we perform. for example, imagine a 100 - node cluster and say one pod has just changed. what happens currently ( which i think is reasonable ) is that all kubelets are listening to pods that are assigned to them. this however translates to opening watch for all pods, and filtering them at the apiserver based on the label / field selectors. this means that the particular change of a pod will be read from etcd 100 times, each time we independently decode it, apply labels and send it ( to at most one kubelet ). note that we're decoding the same pod read from etcd 100 times, which is a clear waste of resources. # proposal my proposal is to create some kind of cache in the apiserver. the approach i am suggesting is : 1. the cache is used only for reading ( writing doesn't read or modify cache ) 2. the cache is storing decoded api objects ( whether we will be storing all objects or just objects of some particular types is tbd ) together with their etcd index ( modifiedindex ) 3. the cache is storing at most one version of the object with a given key ( the newest one ). 4. when we read an object from etcd ( either via get or watch ) we : - send a request to etcd - if the returned version ( response contains modifiedindex value as an explicit field ) is the same as currently stored in cache, we don't need to decode it and simply return the value from the cache - if the returned version is newer ( modifiedindex is monotonically increasing ) we decode it an update the cache with the new version ( the old version ) - if the returned version is older, we simply have a cache miss and decode it without using

Watch flushing in chunked encoder may be inefficient at scale. we currently invoke flush on the http response after every watch event, in order to guarantee clients see watches immediately. that flush impacts throughput at scale, and may result in undesirable context switches in the server process. we should investigate deferred flushes, allowing the client to set an upper latency bound, or automatically adjusting the flush rate due to throughput. in a 8 core benchmark of watch decode performance, it's roughly 25 % faster not to flush than to flush ( 30us per iteration vs 40us per iteration ) - and time spent over 1m in that loop goes from 67 % waiting on syscall to 17 % waiting on sys call, with much more time spent in gc. @ wojtek - t @ kubernetes / sig - scalability

potential issue of API server cache. copy from discussion in https : / / github. com / kubernetes / kubernetes / pull / 23795 # issuecomment - 208176276 > when api server watched a event, it need to insert the event into all watchers'" input " channel, then each watcher has a goroute running in background to pop events from the " input " channel and sent it to the corresponding client. > > since we process event sequentially ( see [ processevent ] ( https : / / github. com / kubernetes / kubernetes / blob / master / pkg / storage / cacher. go # l362 - l363 ) ), if one watcher was blocked due to some reasons, all other watchers will be blocked! we can ensure correctness by terminating this blocked watcher if it timeout ( 5 seconds ) though, it may make watch really slow. for example, if we have 100 watcher watching a key, 10 watchers blocked and timeout by some reasons, the remaining watchers will receive the event after 50 seconds! may be artificial and speculative though, @ wojtek - t will send a pr to address this

Implement watch at apiserver level. implementing should give us significant performance improvements, because : - we avoid sending multiple watch requests to etcd that send as huge amount of unnecessary data ( e. g. currently all kubelets are watching for pods, but since filtering is done at the apiserver level, there are o ( # nodes ) watches to etcd open all the time, each of them sending all pods ) - on top of that we can build some indexer - see https : / / github. com / googlecloudplatform / kubernetes / issues / 4817 # issuecomment - 89437368 for more details cc @ lavalamp @ davidopp @ bprashanth @ timothysc

title: apiserver: consistent read fallback to etcd can overload apiserver and etcd when watch cache is behind
body:
## What happened

When the watch cache is temporarily behind etcd for more than 3 seconds, a consistent LIST read that would normally be served from cache can fall back to a direct etcd LIST.

Relevant code paths:
- [watch cache 3s wait window](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go#L48-L53)
- [watch cache timeout returns [INLINE_CODE]](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go#L446-L489)
- [consistent LIST fallback to etcd](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/delegator.go#L218-L224)

This becomes dangerous in degraded situations such as:
- etcd defragmentation
- leader re-election
- transient member stall
- delayed watch delivery

## Real-world impact

This failure mode was summarized well by @serathius:

> Consistent read from cache fallback, works great until defrag. 
> Defrag stalls member, watch gets delayed more than 3s, watch cache falls back reads to etcd. 
> Due to lack of APF protection (not aware of fallback), memory jumps, for 2GB pods resource we get: 
> Etcd 17GB->180GB 
> API server 50GB->160GB

This matches the current behavior: a request that is initially expected to be a cheap cache-backed consistent LIST read can become an expensive etcd LIST at runtime once the watch cache is still behind after the 3 second wait window.

## A graceful degradation may be safer

If the cache has not caught up within 3 seconds, etcd and/or apiserver are likely already under stress. In that situation, bypassing the cache and sending more expensive LIST traffic directly to etcd can make things much worse.

Kube-apiserver already has precedent for returning [INLINE_CODE] under degraded watch cache conditions. For example, when the watch cache is not ready, LIST requests can already be rejected with [INLINE_CODE]:
- [existing [INLINE_CODE] on unready watch cache](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L763-L768)

## Proposed direction

One possible direction would be to introduce a feature gate for this fallback path.

When enabled, if a consistent LIST read cannot be served from watch cache within the current 3 second wait window, kube-apiserver would return [INLINE_CODE] with [INLINE_CODE] instead of falling back to etcd. This would let clients retry later, rather than turning a cache-backed read into an expensive etcd LIST while the system is already degraded.

The reasoning is:
- if the cache is behind for more than 3 seconds, etcd and/or kube-apiserver are likely already under stress
- turning a cheap cache read into an expensive etcd LIST is risky
- asking clients to retry may give etcd time to recover and the watch cache time to catch up
- once the cache catches up again, the same consistent LIST can be served safely from cache

Using a feature gate would preserve backward compatibility and keep the current fallback-to-etcd behavior as the default, while allowing operators to opt into a safer graceful-degradation mode for large or sensitive clusters.

send a request to etcd - if the returned version ( response contains modifiedindex value as an explicit field ) is the same as currently stored in cache, we don't need to decode it and simply return the value from the cache - if the returned version is newer ( modifiedindex is monotonically increasing ) we decode it an update the cache with the new version ( the old version ) - if the returned version is older, we simply have a cache miss and decode it without using
Add a simple master benchmark and a wrapper to run it.. it's better than nothing, @ lavalamp @ davidopp thoughts? i do plan to shove etcd in a cgroup and use more kubectl libraries in test _ utils.

title: Job controller manageJob() returns active=0 during backoff, causing "cannot set more ready pods than active" status update rejection
body:
### What happened?

When the Job controller's [INLINE_CODE] function determines that replacement pods are needed but a backoff timer is active (due to recent pod failures), it returns [INLINE_CODE] to the caller. The caller uses this value to set [INLINE_CODE] in a status update, while [INLINE_CODE] retains the real informer-computed count. The apiserver validation [INLINE_CODE] (GA in 1.33 via [INLINE_CODE]) correctly rejects this inconsistent update with 422.

Because the status update fails, the controller cannot:
- Flush [INLINE_CODE]
- Remove [INLINE_CODE] finalizers from terminated pods

This causes pods to appear stuck in Terminating state and job status to become stale.

**Root cause:** Two locations in [INLINE_CODE] return a hardcoded [INLINE_CODE] instead of the real [INLINE_CODE] count when backoff is active:

[CODE_BLOCK]

The caller sets [INLINE_CODE] (the returned 0), while [INLINE_CODE] stays at the informer count (e.g., 5). Result: [INLINE_CODE] → 422.

The [INLINE_CODE] was likely a "don't care" value from before [INLINE_CODE] validation existed. Every other return path in [INLINE_CODE] returns the real active count.

### What did you expect to happen?

The backoff early-return in [INLINE_CODE] should return the real active pod count (unchanged, since no pods were created or deleted), not 0.

Proposed fix:
[CODE_BLOCK]

Returning [INLINE_CODE] (initialized at top of [INLINE_CODE] as [INLINE_CODE]) means "I didn't create or delete any pods" — the correct semantics for a backoff deferral.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

[CODE_BLOCK]

### Anything else we need to know?

- The bug fires on any multi-pod Job that experiences a pod failure while other pods are still Ready. For single failures (10s backoff), it produces a few 422 errors that self-resolve. For mass failures (spot reclamation, node failure → backoff capped at 10 min), it causes visible stuck pods and stale status for the full backoff duration.
- No data loss occurs. The job eventually completes. The impact is operational: stuck Terminating pods, stale status, KCM error log spam.
- The [INLINE_CODE] label on the return is also incorrect (no pods were created), but that's cosmetic.

Bug present from 1.31 (when [INLINE_CODE] was introduced, beta default-on) through latest master. Unconditional from 1.33 ([INLINE_CODE] GA).

Tested and reproduced on 1.35.

title: [Feature Request] Native Zone/Topology-Aware Scaling in HPA to complement Topology Aware Routing
body:
### What would you like to be added?

### Description
When combining **Topology Aware Routing** ([INLINE_CODE]) with the **HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA)**, there is a systemic architectural gap that risks localized pod starvation during scale-out events, and extreme endpoint imbalance during scale-in events. 

Currently, the HPA evaluates resource utilization (e.g., CPU, Memory) as a global, deployment-wide aggregate average. However, Topology Aware Routing deliberately isolates traffic to localized Availability Zones (AZs). 

This decoupled behavior creates a "Thundering Herd" trap during spikes, and a "Starvation" trap during downscaling, because the network routing layer is highly topology-aware while the autoscaling control loop is completely topology-blind.

### Why is this needed?

### Use Case
We run high-throughput microservices on AWS (EKS) distributed across 3 Availability Zones. To mitigate high cross-AZ data transfer costs ("Cross-AZ Tax") and lower network latency, we rely heavily on Topology Aware Routing. 

We face two distinct structural failures due to the lack of zone-aware autoscaling:

1. **The Scale-Out Trap (Localized Overload):** During localized network shifts or zone-specific traffic spikes, pods in a single AZ (e.g., [INLINE_CODE]) take 100% of that localized load. If [INLINE_CODE] pods hit 95% CPU utilization while pods in [INLINE_CODE] and [INLINE_CODE] remain idle at 10%, the cluster-wide average sits at ~38%. The HPA fails to trigger, and the pods in the stressed zone crash due to localized resource starvation.
2. **The Scale-In Trap (Zone Depletion):** When traffic drops globally and the HPA triggers a downscale event, the underlying ReplicaSet controller selects pods for termination without respecting zone distribution. It frequently terminates a disproportionate number of pods from a single zone. This leaves that specific zone entirely depleted of endpoints, breaking the path for subsequent localized traffic and forcing expensive, high-latency cross-AZ failovers.

### Proposed Solution / Architectural Approaches
We request native support for zone/topology-awareness within the core autoscaling and lifecycle framework:

1. **Topology-Aware Scale-Out Policy:** Introduce a configuration field in the HPA spec (e.g., [INLINE_CODE]) that evaluates metrics per topology domain. If *any single zone* breaches the target utilization threshold, the HPA should proactively trigger a scale-up event.
2. **Topology-Aware Scale-In (Downscaling):** Ensure that when the HPA reduces the replica count, the scale-in mechanism balances pod terminations proportionally across all active topology domains. The controller must prevent downscaling from leaving a specific zone starved of healthy endpoints.
3. **Handling Soft Constraints ([INLINE_CODE]):** If a deployment utilizes [INLINE_CODE], a Zone-Aware HPA should exploit this flexibility. During a localized spike, it should scale up replicas specifically within the hurting topology domain, allowing a temporary skew to absorb the traffic. During the subsequent scale-in event, the controller must prioritize deleting pods from the skewed zone to automatically return the cluster to its baseline balanced topology spread.

### Related Existing Issue
* **kubernetes/kubernetes #124149** 

### Additional Context
Current ecosystem workarounds require engineers to deploy entirely independent, duplicated Deployments and HPAs per AZ (e.g., [INLINE_CODE], [INLINE_CODE]). This completely breaks standard GitOps principles, bloat CI/CD pipelines, and forces rigid, static replica constraints. Native lifecycle zone-awareness is required to bridge the gap between how Kubernetes routes traffic and how it manages compute capacity.

title: EasyCLA blocks website main to dev branch-sync PRs on kubernetes-prow[bot] merge commits
body:
### What happened?

Weekly "Merge main branch into dev-1.37" sync PRs against [INLINE_CODE] fail the **EasyCLA** check with [INLINE_CODE], and the only committer flagged is the bot identity [INLINE_CODE].

These sync PRs merge [INLINE_CODE] into the release dev branch, which by design pulls in the merge commits that Prow created when merging earlier PRs. title: Watch client shutdown: three remaining bugs from #131505
body:
In 2025 I fixed several watch client shutdown bugs: #131266 (reflector Stop deadlock), #131321 (VeryShortWatchError), #131706 (watch test body cleanup). Thanks again to @wojtek-t and @liggitt for those reviews.

The test work in #131505 turned up three more bugs. They were documented there as TODOs but never fixed. I've verified all three still exist on master (843726939e9) and plan to send one small PR per bug:

1. **Response body leak.** [INLINE_CODE] doesn't close [INLINE_CODE] when content-type negotiation fails. Tracked in #140464.

2. **Error event after Stop.** [INLINE_CODE] selects between the done channel and the error send. When both are ready Go picks at random, so a decode error racing with [INLINE_CODE] reaches the consumer about half the time. First reported back in 2015 (#6433) and again recently in #139782. The open fix #139783 adds the http2 error string to [INLINE_CODE], which helps that case, but the race allows any decode error through after Stop. My PR will check the done channel first so a stopped watcher just closes its result channel.

3. **Broken error unwrapping.** [INLINE_CODE] and the client watch decoder wrap decode errors with [INLINE_CODE], which severs [INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE]. Consumers end up string-matching the message. Config Sync, for example, matches the literal "unable to decode an event from the watch stream: context canceled" text to detect shutdown. Small enough to fix without its own issue.

Each PR is small, structured as a failing test commit followed by the fix, with race detector and stress output in the description.

Requesting [INLINE_CODE] so the fix PRs land against accepted issues.

/sig api-machinery

title: [Failing Test] pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master failing on all PRs: VM provisioning can't install OpenSSH (WU error 0x80244022)
body:
### Which jobs are failing?

pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master

### Which tests are failing?

None. The job dies during Azure VM provisioning, before checking out or testing anything. Zero test results are produced.

### Since when has it been failing?

Since at least 2026-07-23 ~16:00 UTC. The prow job history shows 0 successes across all PRs since then (a mix of FAILURE and ABORTED); before that the job was mostly green with occasional flakes.

### Testgrid link

https://prow.k8s.io/job-history/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/directory/pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The harness ([INLINE_CODE]) installs OpenSSH on the freshly provisioned Windows VM via [INLINE_CODE], which pulls the capability from Windows Update. That call is failing on every VM:

[CODE_BLOCK]

[INLINE_CODE] is [INLINE_CODE]: the VM cannot reach Windows Update (or WU is returning 503). As a result sshd is never installed:

[CODE_BLOCK]

Every run fails identically on a different VM/IP, so this is not a flake; it is either a Windows Update/Azure-side outage or an image/network change affecting the harness's WU access.

Example runs (from kubernetes/kubernetes#140882, three consecutive failures with identical signature):

- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/140882/pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master/2080325276394328064
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/140882/pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master/2080328164998909952
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/140882/pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master/2080330379864051712

### Anything else we need to know?

The job is in the required presubmit set, so this blocks merges on every kubernetes/kubernetes PR. Hardening options regardless of the upstream outage: bake the OpenSSH capability into the VM image instead of installing it from Windows Update at provision time, or add retry/fallback (e.g. the Win32-OpenSSH release zip) in [INLINE_CODE].

title: HPA shows integer underflow value (-9223372036854775808m) for AverageValue metric targets when replicas is 0
body:
### What happened?

When a workload is scaled down to 0 replicas (with KEDA for instance), the HPA controller attempts to calculate the average metric value (total metric / 0 replicas). This division by zero causes the HPA's [INLINE_CODE] to underflow to [INLINE_CODE](math.MinInt64) and, if the scaling becomes then inactive, gets stuck with this underflow value in the HPA object.

### What did you expect to happen?

When the workload replica count is 0, skip the per-pod average calculation. The HPA controller should bypass the division step when statusReplicas == 0 and return the total raw metric value as a fallback.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Configure an HPA with an External metric and target type AverageValue
- Scale the workload up to at least 1 replica so the HPA performs a metric evaluation
- Scale the workload down to 0 replicas
- Check the HPA status using kubectl get hpa (or -o yaml)

I have made a script to reproduce this with KEDA in https://gist.github.com/KengoA/65599c5ffd635c5e1c1c783502a7d340 which I ran on a GKE cluster. I have the full stdout from the script in the gist, but it gets into a state like the following (replicas is shown as 5 here when I printed the output but this becomes 0 after a few seconds):
[CODE_BLOCK]

This is also reported in https://github.com/kedacore/keda/issues/5730 with other users facing a similar issue, and the overflow/underflow issue is identified by in https://github.com/kedacore/keda/issues/5730#issuecomment-2247692693.

### Anything else we need to know?

The zero division and then underflow issue seems to happen on GKE clusters which I replicated above. I saw moments of overflow during transient phases.

Note that this does not affect the autoscaling behaviour itself as this only happens when replica is 0.

title: gofmt in go1.26.5 gives different output on amd64 and arm64, which breaks ci-kubernetes-verify-master-canary
body:
### Which jobs are failing?

ci-kubernetes-verify-master-canary (the only verify job that runs on arm64 nodes, on the AKS build cluster)

### Which tests are failing?

verify-gofmt.sh

### Since when has it been failing?

First failure 2026-07-20 17:12 UTC, a few hours after #140000 merged. The job then alternated between green and red depending on which node it landed on. It has failed every run since 2026-07-29 17:06 UTC because every pod since then has landed on arm64 nodes.

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-k8s-infra-canaries#verify-master-canary

### Reason for failure (if possible)

gofmt from go1.26.5 does not produce the same output on amd64 and arm64 for one struct literal in [INLINE_CODE] (added in #140000). The amd64 build of gofmt accepts the code as checked in. The arm64 build wants the short fields aligned to the long [INLINE_CODE] line. Each build rejects the form the other one wants, so running update-gofmt cannot produce a form both accept.

This is a bug in Go, not in the release binaries. The gofmt binaries in the CI image match the official go.dev tarballs, and building gofmt from unmodified go1.26.5 sources reproduces the difference purely by changing GOARCH. The cause is in go/printer, which decides where to break column alignment using a geometric mean computed with [INLINE_CODE] and [INLINE_CODE] (nodes.go lines 232 to 287 in go1.26.5). Those functions can differ in the last bit between architectures, and the field lengths in this literal sit exactly on the 2.5 ratio threshold, so the decision flips. Presubmits run on amd64, which is why the change merged cleanly.

Evidence: the last green run (build 2082497666687700992, amd64 node) and the first red run of the streak (build 2082513014723973120, arm64 node) tested the same commit 7fbcad5e8ec.

### Anything else we need to know?

The fix on our side is to restructure the literal so the long field is assigned after the struct is built. I verified that form is accepted by gofmt from go1.26.5 on linux amd64, linux arm64, and darwin arm64, and by go1.27rc2. I will send a PR and file a golang/go issue for the printer bug.

title: Kubernetes ships etcd 3.6.6-0 with 61 CVEs (2 Critical) across all supported versions — upstream 3.7.1 available
body:
/sig cluster-lifecycle
/sig etcd
/kind bug
/priority critical-urgent

## Summary

All currently supported Kubernetes versions (v1.34.x, v1.35.x, v1.36.x)
ship [INLINE_CODE], which contains **61 known
vulnerabilities** in the etcd binary alone including **2 Critical**.
The upstream etcd project has released v3.7.1.

etcd 3.6.6-0 has the **oldest dependencies of any Kubernetes control
plane component**, compiled with Go 1.24.10 and gRPC 1.71.1.

## Confirmed Across All Supported K8s Versions
[CODE_BLOCK]

## Scan Results
[CODE_BLOCK]

## CRITICAL Vulnerabilities

| CVE | Library | Installed | Fixed | Title |
|-----|---------|-----------|-------|-------|
| CVE-2026-33186 | google.golang.org/grpc | **v1.71.1** | 1.79.3 | **gRPC-Go: Authorization bypass due to improper HTTP/2 path validation** |
| CVE-2025-68121 | Go stdlib | **v1.24.10** | 1.24.13 | **Incorrect certificate validation during TLS session resumption** |

**Both are directly exploitable in etcd:**
- etcd IS a gRPC server — gRPC is its primary communication protocol
- etcd uses mTLS for peer-to-peer and client communication

## etcd-Specific CVEs 

etcd 3.6.6 has additional CVEs due to its older Go stdlib (1.24.10):

| CVE | Severity | Title |
|-----|----------|-------|
| CVE-2025-61726 | HIGH | Memory exhaustion in net/url query parameter parsing |
| CVE-2025-61729 | HIGH | DoS via excessive resource consumption in crypto/x509 |
| CVE-2025-61727 | MEDIUM | x509 subdomain constraint doesn't restrict wildcard SANs |
| CVE-2025-61728 | MEDIUM | Excessive CPU in archive/zip |
| CVE-2025-61730 | MEDIUM | TLS handshake messages at incorrect encryption level |
| CVE-2025-47913 | HIGH | SSH client panic (x/crypto 0.36.0 specific) |
| CVE-2025-47914 | MEDIUM | SSH Agent DoS via malformed messages |
| CVE-2025-58181 | MEDIUM | DoS via unbounded GSSAPI memory consumption |
| CVE-2025-47911 | MEDIUM | Quadratic HTML parsing complexity |
| CVE-2025-58190 | MEDIUM | Infinite HTML parsing loop |

## Impact

etcd stores **all Kubernetes cluster state** including secrets,
configmaps, RBAC policies, and service accounts. A compromise of
etcd means complete cluster compromise. The CRITICAL gRPC
authorization bypass (CVE-2026-33186) and TLS certificate
validation failure (CVE-2025-68121) in the component that guards
all cluster data is an urgent concern.

## Request

1. **Bump etcd to 3.7.1** (or latest compatible) in upcoming
 patch releases for v1.35.x and v1.36.x
2. If 3.7.x has compatibility concerns, at minimum bump to a
 newer 3.6.x patch (if one exists with updated dependencies)
3. Is there a tracking issue for etcd version updates?

## How to Reproduce

```bash
trivy image registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.6-0

title: DeviceTaintRule with deviceSelector omitted blocks device allocation cluster-wide, including adminAccess claims, contradicting documented behavior
body:
### What happened?

A [INLINE_CODE] with the [INLINE_CODE] field entirely omitted (not an empty [INLINE_CODE] object
-- the field itself absent) makes every device on every node, across every driver and pool,
untolerated and therefore unschedulable -- not just whatever devices the taint was meant to
target.

Live-verified on a freshly-created kind cluster running v1.37.0 GA with **no non-default
feature gates set at all** ([INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE]
are all GA and enabled by default at this release):

1. An ordinary [INLINE_CODE] targeting one device ([INLINE_CODE]) allocates and its Pod runs, with
 zero [INLINE_CODE]s present.
2. Apply a [INLINE_CODE] with [INLINE_CODE] and [INLINE_CODE] omitted:
 [CODE_BLOCK]
3. The exact same claim/Pod from step 1, recreated, now fails to schedule ([INLINE_CODE],
 [INLINE_CODE]).
4. Also confirmed on a 4-device pool: every device becomes unschedulable, not just one --
 including a claim declaring [INLINE_CODE], which is otherwise documented to bypass
 ordinary device exclusivity but is not exempted from [INLINE_CODE] enforcement.
5. Deleting only the [INLINE_CODE] (no other change) immediately restores every
 previously-blocked claim to allocate successfully.

### What did you expect to happen?

According to the field's own documentation ([INLINE_CODE]):

> The empty selector matches all devices. Without a selector, no devices are matches [sic].

A [INLINE_CODE] with [INLINE_CODE] omitted should match **zero** devices and have no
scheduling effect -- the opposite of what actually happens.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a cluster running v1.37.0 (no special feature gates required).
2. Install any DRA driver advertising at least one device (repro used
 [INLINE_CODE] v0.4.0).
3. Create an ordinary [INLINE_CODE] + Pod referencing one device; confirm it runs.
4. Apply a [INLINE_CODE] with any [INLINE_CODE] and [INLINE_CODE] omitted entirely.
5. Observe: any *new* claim against *any* device in the cluster -- including unrelated
 drivers/pools, and [INLINE_CODE] claims -- fails to schedule.
6. Delete the [INLINE_CODE]; confirm previously-blocked claims immediately allocate.

### Anything else we need to know?

- This appears specific to the [INLINE_CODE] enforcement path. Tested [INLINE_CODE] separately: a
 [INLINE_CODE] [INLINE_CODE] with [INLINE_CODE] omitted does **not** evict an already-running
 pod on an unrelated device (its [INLINE_CODE] condition stays [INLINE_CODE]
 indefinitely) -- confirmed the eviction mechanism itself works correctly in the same environment
 via a positive control (a [INLINE_CODE] taint with a matching selector evicted the target pod
 within 5 seconds). So the nil-selector matching bug looks confined to whatever code path
 [INLINE_CODE] uses to block new allocation, not the separate eviction controller.
- Distinct from #141422 / the pending fix in #141425: that issue concerns a selector that is
 *present but empty* ([INLINE_CODE]). This report is about the field being *absent*
 entirely -- confirmed by reading #141425's diff that its new validation only rejects the
 empty-but-present case and returns immediately with no error when the selector is nil, so it
 does not cover this scenario.
- Creating a [INLINE_CODE] is a cluster-scoped permission not granted by any built-in
 [INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE] ClusterRole -- but this bug means anyone holding that permission can
 silently take down DRA scheduling cluster-wide with one missing field, when the documented
 default behavior should be a no-op.

title: Reconcile cloud-provider InstanceMetadata.AdditionalLabels periodically
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The cloud node controller should periodically reconcile node labels returned through [INLINE_CODE] for already initialized Nodes.

The reconciliation should:

* add labels that are missing from the Node;
* update labels whose values differ from the current instance metadata;
* preserve unrelated Node labels;
* continue rejecting labels in Kubernetes-reserved namespaces;
* not remove labels that are no longer returned by the cloud provider.

A proposed implementation is available in:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141616

Provider-side implementation:

https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider-openstack/pull/3166

Previous implementation attempts:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130888
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131096

### Why is this needed?

[INLINE_CODE] are currently applied only during the initial synchronization of a Node carrying the external cloud-provider taint.

Consequently, labels introduced by a newer cloud provider are not added to already initialized Nodes, manually removed labels are not restored, and changed values remain stale.

One example is the OpenStack [INLINE_CODE], which identifies the physical compute host within a project. An OpenStack operator may live-migrate an instance while draining a hypervisor for maintenance. In this case, the provider returns a new [INLINE_CODE], but the existing Node label is not updated.

For [INLINE_CODE] implementations, the cloud node controller already periodically calls [INLINE_CODE]. Reconciling [INLINE_CODE] therefore does not require an additional cloud-provider API request.

Existing Pods are not automatically rescheduled when a topology label changes. Updating the label still makes the current placement observable and ensures newly scheduled Pods use the current topology information.

/sig cloud-provider
/area cloudprovider

title: Dynamic Resource Allocation (DeviceClass/Device) is not supported on Windows nodes
body:
# DRA (structured parameters) is not supported on Windows nodes

## What would you like to be added?
Support for Dynamic Resource Allocation - **structured parameters** (KEP-4381; [INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE]) - on Windows nodes, defined by a real Windows enhancement KEP and a Windows-specific device-assignment design. Today the kubelet's Windows container manager stubs every DRA accessor to nil and registers only the device-plugin handler.

## Why is this needed?
DRA exists because the device-plugin + extended-resource model only advertises an integer count of a node-local resource. It cannot express device init/cleanup (e.g. reprogramming an FPGA), partial partitions (Nvidia MIG / SR-IOV), dynamic/network-attached devices, or structured property-based matching. The motivating scenario - device-centric accelerator workloads (GPU/AI, NIC/DPU, edge/batch) - applies to Windows containers exactly as on Linux (Windows GPU/AI is a real, growing use case). So the gap is real and worth closing.

## KEP status (source-verified)
- Base DRA today is **KEP-4381 (structured parameters)**, not KEP-3063. KEP-3063 (the original 'classic' DRA) was **withdrawn** in Kubernetes 1.32 and its code removed; #4381 now defines the base functionality and driver interface.
- The Windows TODO in the code references [INLINE_CODE], which **does not exist** (no such KEP in kubernetes/enhancements; no Windows-DRA KEP in the sig-windows index). So DRA-on-Windows is not only unimplemented but also untracked.

## Current state (source-verified)
- [INLINE_CODE] [INLINE_CODE]: [INLINE_CODE]; only the device-plugin handler is registered.
- DRA accessors are stubs on Windows: [INLINE_CODE] -> nil, [INLINE_CODE] -> nil, [INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE] -> nil.

## Why the Linux design does not apply as-is
- Linux DRA injects devices via **CDI** (/dev + mount + runtime config) into the container; Prepare/Unprepare stage host devices. This depends on Linux /dev/mount/CDI semantics.
- In process-isolated (shared-kernel) Windows containers there is no /dev tree and no mount-based CDI injection; device exposure is per-Job-Object / device-interface / GPU-PV handle. The CDI mechanism is not portable.

## Recommended new design for Windows
Because the same scenario occurs on Windows and a viable mechanism exists, this issue is kept open. Proposed Windows-specific model under KEP-4381 structured parameters:
1. **Reuse the control plane unchanged**: the existing [INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE] API + scheduler-side allocation. No API divergence.
2. **Device injection - the real difference**: replace CDI + /dev-mount with **per-Job-Object / container device assignment**:
 - GPU: assign the Windows GPU adapter / device-interface (GPU-PV surface) to the container.
 - Generic: expose device handles into the container's Object Manager namespace (host-process sidecar or per-Job-Object device-permission model).
3. **Prepare/Unprepare map to Windows APIs**: open/close handles + device lease, not mount/unmount.
4. **podresources**: [INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE] surface the assigned device + claim, matching the contract.

## Next steps
- Open a real **Windows DRA enhancement KEP** (under the KEP-4381 structured-parameters model) covering registration, claim prepare/unprepare, and device exposure on Windows - the referenced kep.k8s.io/4680 does not exist.
- Get sig/windows + sig-node + sig/apps direction on device-assignment vs reusing devicemanager plumbing.
- Implement the DRA accessors and wire DRA device registration, replacing the stubs.

## For triage (labels wanted)
Please add [INLINE_CODE], [INLINE_CODE], [INLINE_CODE] for discovery (the filing account cannot add them; they are applied via [INLINE_CODE] and [INLINE_CODE] commands).

## Environment
k8s master. Evidence: [INLINE_CODE] (handler), [INLINE_CODE] (GetAllocatableDevices nil), [INLINE_CODE] (DRA stubs); base DRA: KEP-4381; Windows isolation: MS Learn.

---
AI-assisted analysis; verified against source; corrected to the KEP-4381 structured-parameters base (KEP-3063 withdrawn). Reconcile with sig/windows + sig-node maintainers.

Why this is "overdue": Both gates hit GA + LockToDefault: true in 1.34. Per the file's own policy header:
 
"To support n-3 compatibility version, features may only be removed 3 releases after graduation."
 
GA was 1.34 → eligible for removal starting 1.37. Master is currently developing ~1.38 (other entries show alpha: v1.37 already shipped), so we're now 1+ releases past the earliest allowed removal point — these gates are stale/overdue cleanup, exactly the kind the "20+ overdue feature gates" metric flags.
 
How to fix — a cleanup PR that:
 
1. Removes the WinDSR / WinOverlay constants from pkg/features/kube_features.go 
2. Removes their VersionedSpecs map entries (shown above)
3. Removes/unconditionalizes any utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(kubefeatures.WinDSR/WinOverlay) checks — most likely in pkg/proxy/winkernel/proxier.go — since the feature is always-on, that code path becomes the only path
4. Updates any e2e test skip/feature annotations ( test/e2e/windows/... ) that still reference the gate names
5. Send as /kind cleanup , sig/windows , referencing KEP-5100 as context

clean up

title: Namespace-scoped `RoleBinding` can grant write permissions on the namespace itself
body:
### What happened?

In a multi-tenant cluster where individual tenants get full control of a specific namespace, e.g. via binding to a [INLINE_CODE] like [INLINE_CODE] using a rule with all-wildcard matches, tenants may also edit and delete that namespace. This is in spite of namespaces themselves being a cluster-scoped resource.

In a fresh cluster created via [INLINE_CODE], a [INLINE_CODE] for the tenant to a [INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE] that allows creating [INLINE_CODE] (e.g. the default [INLINE_CODE] [INLINE_CODE]) is sufficient as the user can escalate their privileges by binding to any [INLINE_CODE] that grants write permissions on namespaces.

### What did you expect to happen?

A namespace-scoped [INLINE_CODE]-granted permission should not allow editing and deleting a cluster-scoped namespace resource.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

In a fresh cluster, e.g. created via kind, run the following set of commands:
[CODE_BLOCK]

### Anything else we need to know?

This was brought up before in #134929 framed around service accounts, but the issue applies universally. It was rejected due to being intended behavior, an assessment I disagree with.

Namespaces *are* cluster-scoped resources and it's very unintuitive and unexpected that a namespace-scoped [INLINE_CODE] grants permissions on such a resource. Clusters without additional validating policies are in a less-secure state by default with this behavior. Further privilege escalation e.g. by adjusting pod security standards via namespace labels is possible in this way.

As a cluster admin, I expect that I can control things on a namespace level via the [INLINE_CODE] object without tenants interfering with this *in any scenario*.

As far as I can tell, this behavior is also not documented anywhere, at least I couldn't find anything on the [RBAC documentation page](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac) where I'd expect this kind of behavior to be called out in a warning.

title: Billing can be bypassed using a combination of subagents with an agent definition, resulting in unlimited free premium requests.
body:
## Summary

It's possible in Copilot to bypass any billing / 'premium request' usage by taking advantage of:
- Subagents and tool calls not consuming any 'requests'.
- Request cost being calculated on the initial model used.
- "Free" models incl. in Copilot e.g. GPT-5-mini, GPT-4.1 etc.
- Ability to define an agent for a subagent.
- Ability to specify a model for an agent.

Combining these correctly results in 'free' and almost unlimited, usage of expensive premium models like Opus 4.5 which would usually cost '3 premium requests':

## Instructions

1. Start a new Chat.
2. Set the model to a "free" model, included in Copilot e.g. GPT-5 Mini.
3. Create an agent, and set it's model to a premium model, e.g. Opus 4.5
4. Set the mode to "agent".
5. In the initial message, instruct it to launch an agent '[your_agents_name_here]' as a subagent using the runSubagent tool, and to pass on the following query e.g. "What time is it in London, UK".
6. Submit the message.
7. The initial request will be picked up by the free GPT-5 Mini model, incurring no fees.
8. The free model will create a subagent (which is also free)
9. The free subagent will launch with an 'agent' profile, this profile has the model set to a premium model
10. The premium model will be used for the subagent - but premium requests will be consumed.

## Example 1

**Example Chat Message:**
[CODE_BLOCK]

---

**Example Prompt File:**
[INLINE_CODE]

[CODE_BLOCK]

---

**Example Agent File**
[INLINE_CODE]

[CODE_BLOCK]

---

## Example 2

Another vector for abuse - albeit requiring more effort is:
- Set [INLINE_CODE] to a high value.
- Use a premium model e.g. Opus 4.5 as the initial model for the chat session.
- Build a custom script (not disclosed for safety), that you tell the model to call as part of a tool invocation.
- Craft some prompts to direct the model to repeat the tool call(s).
- The right script, with the right prompts can be tailored to create a loop, allowing the premium model to continually be invoked unlimited times for no additional cost beyond that of the initial message. 

In my testing I had a single message result in a 3hr+ process that launched hundreds of Opus 4.5 subagents to process hundreds of files - and only consumed 3 premium credits. Had I not stopped it at 3hrs, it would have continued.

---

**Related**: I also noted the message 'types' are being declared on the client, inferring no API validation e.g: https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-copilot-chat/blob/main/src/extension/intents/node/toolCallingLoop.ts#L484

I believe this is another vector that allows for more blatant abuse directly against the API.

---

**Note**: Initially submitted this to MSRC (VULN-172488), MSRC insisted bypassing billing is outside of MSRC scope and instructed me multiple times to file as a public bug report.

---

- VS Code Version: 1.109.0-insider (Universal) - f3d99dee2f4c63061a08f828e0ca6b6acf6ac0f8
- OS Version: OSX Tahoe 26.3
- Feature: Agent / SubAgent

This is NOT the same issue as https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/252230
(My previous issue was auto closed by the bot and deferred to the above).

title: Terminal processes accumulate unboundedly during Copilot Agent sessions, causing OOM crashes on Windows + WSL
body:
Type: Bug VS Code Version 1.109.5 (Stable) OS Version Windows (128 GB RAM) with WSL2 (Ubuntu, configured for 96 GB via .wslconfig) Extensions GitHub Copilot + GitHub Copilot Chat (latest stable) ms-python.python, Pylance, Ruff, Jupyter, Remote-WSL, PowerShell (Full list: ~26 recommended extensions, see below) Reproducible Yes — occurs every weekend during unattended/long-running Copilot Agent sessions Steps to Reproduce Open a Python workspace with ~2.7 GB on disk and a custom default terminal profile (PowerShell with -NoExit -File dev_shell.ps1). Set "chat.agent.maxRequests": 500 and "chat.tools.terminal.enableAutoApprove": true in workspace settings. Start a Copilot Agent conversation that performs many tool calls involving terminal commands (code searches, test runs, linting, etc.). Leave VS Code running over a weekend with multiple such sessions. Observe that terminal processes accumulate and are never reaped. Actual Behavior After 2-3 days, VS Code has accumulated: 211 PowerShell processes (17.2 GB) 250 conhost.exe processes (2.1 GB) 32 Code.exe renderer/extension host processes (13.2 GB) Total: ~32.6 GB consumed by VS Code alone This causes: Windows OOM kills processes. Both the VS Code extension host and the WSL2 VM (vmmemWSL) can be victims. The WSL2 VM crash kills all WSL-based workloads (TF_1 repository running in Ubuntu/WSL). Both repos crash at different times because the OOM killer is non-deterministic. On restart, VS Code attempts to revive all 211 terminal sessions simultaneously, causing a secondary memory spike. Expected Behavior Terminal processes created by Copilot Agent tool calls should be automatically disposed when the agent turn/conversation ends, or after a configurable idle timeout. There should be a maximum terminal count cap (e.g., terminal.integrated.maxInstances) that prevents unbounded accumulation. When the cap is reached, the oldest idle terminal should be reaped. At minimum, background terminals that have completed their command should not persist indefinitely. Diagnostic Data Current process snapshot (taken while system is stable, not during crash): VS Code ecosystem memory breakdown: Code.exe (32 processes): 13,231 MB PowerShell terminals (211 procs): 17,150 MB conhost.exe (250 processes): 2,079 MB Python (8 processes): 134 MB ───────────────────────────────────────────── TOTAL: 32,594 MB (31.8 GB) WSL: vmmemWSL: 9,502 MB wsl/wslhost/wslrelay (35 procs): 340 MB System: 128 GB total, 45.1 GB used, 82.6 GB free (at time of measurement) Relevant settings: { "chat.agent.maxRequests": 500, "chat.tools.terminal.enableAutoApprove": true, "terminal.integrated.defaultProfile.windows": "Trading-Win Dev Shell", // Custom profile invokes: powershell -NoExit -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File dev_shell.ps1 } Copilot workspace index: local-index.1.db for this workspace: 913 MB (despite extensive github.copilot.chat.indexing.exclude patterns) Workspace on disk: 2.72 GB total (includes 4 Python venvs totaling 1.4 GB, 980 MB of reports, 220 MB .git) .wslconfig: [wsl2] memory=96GB processors=12 swap=32GB localhostForwarding=true gpuSupport=true pageReporting=true Key Observations Each Copilot agent tool call spawns a new terminal process (PowerShell + conhost pair = ~84-90 MB). With maxRequests: 500, a single conversation can spawn 100+ terminal pairs. Terminals are never automatically closed even after the command completes and the agent conversation ends. No built-in terminal count limit exists in VS Code. The terminal panel shows 150+ tabs, and the process tree shows 211 PowerShell + 250 conhost. The 913 MB Copilot local index suggests the indexing excludes are not fully effective, contributing to memory-mapped file pressure. No Windows Event Log entries (Event ID 6008) for unexpected shutdowns in the last 7 days, suggesting the OOM manifests as process kills rather than full system crashes. A pwsh.exe crash was logged on 2/25 with System.InvalidOperationException. Crash Pattern 3 OOM-related crashes over the weekend of Feb 28 - Mar 1, 2026 Both Windows-side (Trading-Win / VS Code) and WSL-side (TF_1) affected Crashes occur at different times, consistent with non-deterministic OOM killer behavior Previous investigation attributed it to Windows side only, but the WSL VM is a secondary victim when Windows reclaims memory by killing the vmmemWSL process Suggested Fixes Add terminal.integrated.maxInstances setting — hard cap on concurrent terminals (default: 50?). Oldest idle terminals auto-disposed when exceeded. Auto-dispose agent terminals — terminals created by Copilot Agent tool calls should be auto-closed when the command completes and output has been read, or when the conversation ends. Add terminal.integrated.idleTimeout setting — auto-close terminals that have been idle for N minutes (e.g., 30 min default). Warn on excessive terminal count — show a notification when terminal count exceeds a threshold (e.g., 50) with an option to close idle ones. Workarounds (for other users hitting this) Reduce chat.agent.maxRequests from 500 to something like 50-100 Periodically run Terminal: Kill All Terminals from the command palette Reduce WSL memory in .wslconfig (e.g., memory=32GB instead of 96GB) to leave headroom for Windows Disable chat.tools.terminal.enableAutoApprove to reduce terminal spawn rate Consider adding a scheduled task to kill old PowerShell processes VS Code version: Code 1.109.5 (072586267e68ece9a47aa43f8c108e0dcbf44622, 2026-02-19T19:43:32.382Z) OS version: Windows_NT x64 10.0.26200 Modes: Remote OS version: Linux x64 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2 Remote OS version: Linux x64 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2 Remote OS version: Linux x64 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2

title: GitHub Copilot "Configure Tools" Popover should show `title` from `serverInfo` for MCP Servers
body: ## Context In GitHub Copilot, you can choose which tools should be available to the agent. In the related "Configure Tools" menu, MCP servers are listed. The UI shows the key of the entry in [INLINE_CODE] as a display name. In case of using an MCP registry when installing servers, this will unfortunately result in rather cryptic names (like [INLINE_CODE]). An MCP Server, in the initialize phase, can communicate it's [INLINE_CODE], including a [INLINE_CODE] and [INLINE_CODE]: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/lifecycle#initialization The general rule in the MCP spec seems to be that, whenever a title is there, it should be prioritized over the (technical) name when displaying it to the UI. It also seems like information from the initialization is already used in the menu, since the GitHub MCP Server features an icon (as announced during initialization), it just doesn't show the name. ## Feature Request If an MCP Server announces a [INLINE_CODE] as part of it's [INLINE_CODE], the "Configure Tools" menu should show the title instead of any technical name (derived from [INLINE_CODE]). The same should also be true in the Chat itself, when the MCP server is used. There, it should also show the corresponding [INLINE_CODE] instead of any technical name. ## Similar Requests - https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/243940 is similar, but focuses on additional instructions in mcp.json - https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/251576 focuses on another part of the UI, i.e. a tooltip for the button that opens the menu this feature talks about

title: Linux apt repo lags behind stable release feed: UI advertises 1.111.0, but packages.microsoft.com only offers 1.110.1
body:
Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Yes

- VS Code Version: 1.110.1 (61b3d0a)
- OS Version: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS x64

Steps to Reproduce:

1. Install stable VS Code on Ubuntu using the official Microsoft apt repository.
2. Run [INLINE_CODE] and check the candidate version with [INLINE_CODE].
3. Open VS Code and check for updates.
4. Observe that VS Code reports a newer stable version is available, while the official Microsoft apt repository still does not publish that version.

Additional information:

VS Code UI reports:
- Current Version: 1.110.1 (61b3d0a)
- Latest Version: 1.111.0 (ce099c1)
- Released Mar 7, 2026

I may be misunderstanding the intended publishing flow on Linux, but from the outside it looks like the stable UI/update feed and the official apt repository are temporarily out of sync.

On this machine, apt still sees only 1.110.1 as the latest available [INLINE_CODE] package.

Local package state:

[CODE_BLOCK]

[CODE_BLOCK]

APT policy for stable [INLINE_CODE]:

[CODE_BLOCK]

[CODE_BLOCK]

APT source configuration:

[CODE_BLOCK]

[CODE_BLOCK]

The direct stable Linux [INLINE_CODE] feed already resolves to 1.111.0:

[CODE_BLOCK]

[CODE_BLOCK]

Expected:
- The official Microsoft apt repository would ideally publish the same stable version that the stable Linux [INLINE_CODE] feed and in-app updater advertise, or the in-app update signal would avoid indicating a newer version before the apt package is available.

Actual:
- In-app updater advertises 1.111.0.
- The direct stable [INLINE_CODE] feed serves 1.111.0.
- The official Microsoft apt repo still offers only 1.110.1 for [INLINE_CODE].

If this delay is expected, it may still be helpful to document it more clearly for Linux apt users, since the UI currently makes it look like an upgrade should already be available through the package manager.

title: Problems pane constantly re-evaluates frontmatter diagnostics for custom agent/instruction/skill/prompt files — excessive CPU and memory
body:
## Environment

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| VS Code | Insiders 1.114.0-insider ([INLINE_CODE]) |
| OS | Linux x86_64 — WSL2 (kernel [INLINE_CODE]), 20 CPUs, 31 GiB RAM |
| GitHub Copilot Chat | v0.42.2026032501 |

Other extensions

[INLINE_CODE] v3.3.10 (declarative extension pack, no JS/TS), [INLINE_CODE] v2026.38.0, [INLINE_CODE] v0.31.2, [INLINE_CODE] v2026.4.0, [INLINE_CODE] v2026.1.1, [INLINE_CODE] v1.24.0, [INLINE_CODE] v4.5.6, [INLINE_CODE] v2.1.2

## Bug

In a workspace with **472 custom Copilot files** (49 [INLINE_CODE], 349 [INLINE_CODE], 11 [INLINE_CODE], 63 [INLINE_CODE]), the [INLINE_CODE] diagnostic collection constantly clears and re-populates frontmatter diagnostics in the Problems pane. The cycle never settles, keeping CPU and memory elevated indefinitely with no user interaction. There is no setting to throttle or disable this behavior.

**Of the 349 [INLINE_CODE] files, 246 are symlinks** in a [INLINE_CODE] directory that resolve back to the same 103 source files in [INLINE_CODE]. The scanner appears to follow symlinks and parse both the source and the link, effectively processing each of those 103 files twice. Only 103 unique [INLINE_CODE] files exist on disk.

**Expected**: diagnostics evaluate once on load/change, then remain stable. Symlinked duplicates should ideally be detected and skipped.

## Root Cause (from extension source inspection)

Three issues combine to create a refresh loop:

1. **No debounce on refresh** — [INLINE_CODE] fires on every [INLINE_CODE] event with no coalescing:

 [CODE_BLOCK]

2. **Full re-parse every time** — [INLINE_CODE] calls [INLINE_CODE] for *every* custom file via [INLINE_CODE], not just changed files. With 472 files (including 246 symlink duplicates) this is expensive.

3. **Cascading events** — after parsing, [INLINE_CODE] fires [INLINE_CODE], which multiple downstream providers (ask-agent, explore-agent, plan-agent, org-agents) listen to. Org agents also **poll** periodically, adding more trigger sources.

## Suggested Mitigations

1. **Debounce** [INLINE_CODE] (e.g., 500ms–2s).
2. **Incremental parsing** — only re-parse changed files.
3. **Break the cascade** — prevent the post-refresh event from triggering another parse round.
4. **Deduplicate symlinks** — resolve symlinks to their canonical path and skip files that have already been parsed.
5. **Add a setting** to control refresh rate or disable frontmatter validation.

## Additional Context

The workspace is [microsoft/hve-core](https://github.com/microsoft/hve-core), which packages agents, instructions, skills, and prompts for VS Code extension distribution. The [INLINE_CODE] directory contains symlinks used during extension packaging — all 246 [INLINE_CODE] files there are symlinks back to the 103 source files in [INLINE_CODE]. An additional 17 transient [INLINE_CODE] plan files in the gitignored [INLINE_CODE] directory increase the scanning surface further during active development sessions.

API for generating embeddings to support local RAG. a common scenario for building custom chat participants is asking information about a specific domain ( platform, framework, tool, etc ). today, the only way to do it, is by exposing an api with semantic search to do rag and get the necessary information, which can be then processed into a user - friendly response using the built - in llms. hosting a semantic search instance typically requires costs, which is beyond reach for some developers. if the built - in lm api exposed and endpoint and a model to compute embeddings for the given string, then developers could do rag via cosine similarity between the embeddings for the user's prompt and pre - computed embeddings for the documents for the specific domain. using this approach, they could retrieve the relevant information from an internal store they can ship with the extension, and pass it for processing to the llm. to ensure that developers can pre - compute embeddings for their documents, ideally, the new endpoint should use a model that developers can run locally, for example using ollama.

title: Copilot Inline Suggestions block IntelliSense suggestions to automatically pop up when pressing letters
body:
**EDIT from @alexdima , project maintainer**: Starting with 1.121.0, we have changed that the suggest widget does not automatically pop up when typing letters. Please see [full rationale below](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/317863#issuecomment-4519342542), but in short we found that the majority of users are faster and manage to create more code that is retained with fewer keystrokes. With the change, the suggest widget still pops up on trigger characters, like [INLINE_CODE] in TS or JS, etc or when manually invoked via [INLINE_CODE]. Nothing has been removed, the previous behavior of automatically popping up the suggest widget is still available, but it is not the default. I apologize if this has caused hassle to you and I realize that the previous behavior was preferable to a subset of users. If you want the previous behavior, just take 10 seconds and configure: [CODE_BLOCK] --- Type: Bug Since the most recent update, I am unable to get IntelliSense without having Inline Suggestions disabled. I looked inside the settings and tried tweaking all sorts of values and I was unable to get the behavior that existed prior. I can confirm disabling Inline Suggestions completely fixes this broken. I found there are 2 new settings for the copilot modal but I cannot enable Next Edit suggestions without "Ghost text suggestions" enabled. (Which I believe is the setting that causes this issue.) I tried disabling all extensions and this issue has persisted for me. 1. Enable Inline Suggestions 2. No more IntelliSense I am not able to enable inline suggestions without ghosting text suggestions. (Next edit suggestions button is greyed out.) My copilot usage is at 100% however this has still worked before. --- EDIT 1: I was able to resolve this issue by pasting in specific settings [CODE_BLOCK] I contacted my other friends regarding this, and the same thing happened to them also, with the same fix (changing the settings). Important to mention, that to one this has happened 3 weeks ago, therefore it is most likely not an issue with the most recent release but something else. --- EDIT 2: I believe this could be the reason this behavior happens: No suggestions are probably not the intended effect. title: "Add Element to Chat" and "Add Console Logs to Chat" no-op when chat panel was closed before
body:
1. Close the chat panel
2. Reload window
3. Use "Add Element to Chat" feature in Integrated Browser (load a website, click on "Add Element to Chat" button, then click on a DOM element on the page)
4. 🐛 The chat panel opens, but it has no attachments
5. Expected: The chat panel should have the selected element as an attachment

The same issue happens with "Add Console Logs to Chat" (but for validating this one, you need to go to a page that has produced console logs)

Important note: It only reproes the first time after reload. Once the panel is loaded, even if you close it, it will work.

[ inline _ code ] then filters the nested array out because it is neither a uri nor an editor commands context, falls back to the active editor group, and attaches the current editor. # # fix spread the arguments ( [ inline _ code ] ) so [ inline _ code ] receives the original argument list. [ inline _ code ] then sees the [ inline _ code ] commands context ( passed by the editor title menu ) and resolves the right - clicked editor. # # test plan - [ ] open two files, make one active - [ ] right - click the non - active tab, pick " add file to chat " - [ ] the non - active file should be attached to the chat ( not the active one ) fixes # 276020

[ inline _ code ] came through as raw text with no changes chip ; [ inline _ code ] lost its file attachment ( # 292064 ). * * how * * — capture [ inline _ code ] and [ inline _ code ] before the clear. after the clear, [ inline _ code ] the text, then re - add both sets via [ inline _ code ] and [ inline _ code ]. finally [ inline _ code ] so the fresh input + restored context flows through the normal submit path. * * test plan * * — new [ inline _ code ] suite : ( 1 ) attachments added before the action persist through to [ inline _ code ] ; ( 2 ) dynamic variable references ( e. g. [ inline _ code ] ) persist through to [ inline _ code ]. manual per the issue : type [ inline _ code ], press ctrl + shift + enter, verify the changes chip + variable decoration appear in the new session. fixes # 292064

title: Agent host CLI: kill_running_server leaks server node child process after upgrade
body:
## Summary

The CLI agent host supervisor's [INLINE_CODE] path leaks the underlying server node process when restarting after a [INLINE_CODE] RPC. The bash launcher script ([INLINE_CODE]) is terminated, but the [INLINE_CODE] child it [INLINE_CODE]'d remains alive as an orphan.

## Repro

Discovered while testing https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/319455 against a remote macOS host using a pinned-old-server CLI:

1. Bring up an agent host supervisor on commit A (e.g. [INLINE_CODE], protocol 0.2.0).
2. Connect a desktop on commit B (newer protocol 0.3.0). Handshake fails with [INLINE_CODE].
3. Click "Update Server". The supervisor receives the [INLINE_CODE] RPC, calls [INLINE_CODE], then restarts on commit B.
4. Observe processes on the remote: the bash wrapper for commit A is gone, but its node child (e.g. [INLINE_CODE]) is still alive with [INLINE_CODE].

In my test run the orphan was pid 230 and survived indefinitely; only the new commit-B server's child was tracked by the supervisor after the restart.

## Suspected cause

[INLINE_CODE] (or the platform-specific kill helper it delegates to) appears to signal the immediate child only. The server launcher is:

[CODE_BLOCK]

Bash does not forward [INLINE_CODE] to its children by default, and we don't wait on it before terminating the new generation, so the node child is reparented to PID 1 and continues running. It does eventually exit when its IPC pipe closes, but in our test it persisted for the duration of the run.

## Suggested fix

A couple of options, in rough order of preference:

1. **Signal the whole process group / job** from the CLI side — i.e. set up the server child in its own process group at spawn time ([INLINE_CODE] / [INLINE_CODE]) and send [INLINE_CODE] to the negative pgid on shutdown. Robust regardless of what the launch script does.
2. **Make the launcher forward signals**, e.g. [INLINE_CODE] [INLINE_CODE] / [INLINE_CODE] in [INLINE_CODE] and re-signal [INLINE_CODE] before [INLINE_CODE]. Cheaper change but doesn't help non-shell launchers.
3. **Replace the bash launcher with a direct exec** so the CLI's child *is* the node server. Simplest of all if there's no other reason to keep the shell shim.

## Scope

- CLI only ([INLINE_CODE] and the server-bin shim at [INLINE_CODE]).
- Independent of https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/319455; that PR fixes the desktop-side reconnect after upgrade, and is unaffected by whether the old server's node child gets reaped cleanly.
- Probably also fires on any non-upgrade shutdown path that goes through [INLINE_CODE] (e.g. supervisor exit / quality switch), so the fix is generally useful.

(Written by Copilot)

title: Add Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite to BYOK known models whitelist
body:
### Summary

Request adding [INLINE_CODE] to the BYOK known models whitelist at https://main.vscode-cdn.net/extensions/copilotChat.json so it can be used via the native Gemini provider with full thinking + tool calling support.

### Motivation

Google's free tier Gemini API offers 500 RPD (Requests Per Day) for [INLINE_CODE], which is significantly higher than other models. This makes it the most practical choice for developers using BYOK with the free tier, enabling sustained coding sessions without hitting rate limits.

- Rate Limits: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits
- Model Specs: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/gemini/3-1-flash-lite

### Current Workaround Limitations

1. **[INLINE_CODE] vendor**: Can connect via Google's OpenAI-compatible endpoint, but fails with thinking models due to missing [INLINE_CODE] support (required by Gemini thinking models for function calling).

2. **Native [INLINE_CODE] vendor**: Correctly handles [INLINE_CODE] but filters models against the remote whitelist ([INLINE_CODE]), which currently does not include [INLINE_CODE].
